paragraphs.text: All creation proclaims the mercy and love of God for humankind, and so does the ordering of creation. There is nothing in the visible world that does not proclaim God's goodness. Heaven, earth, sea and all things visible and invisible came into being, hold together and are preserved by the mercy of God. So it is fitting that blessed David proclaims the Merciful One on account of his love for humankind, saying: "The Lord is merciful and righteous, and our God shows mercy."

He blended righteousness with love for humankind, calling God both righteous and loving, so that when you hear "righteous" you may fear the judgment, and when you hear "loving" you may run to repentance. He does not proclaim love unqualified, nor righteousness on its own. If he proclaimed only righteousness, he would drive to despair those who hope in mercy; and if he spoke only of love for humankind, he would lead the more careless to contempt. "The Lord God is merciful, compassionate and righteous." He joined love for humankind to righteousness, but he placed mercy at the beginning of his words and as their seal at the end.

For all things began from love for humankind and ended in love for humankind. Heaven came into being out of love for humankind, not because God needed it. Not yet six thousand years have passed since heaven was created. But before the heavens, and before those ages that are boundless and without beginning, God is and was; and the word "was" is spoken of him before every conception of the mind. So heaven did not come into being because God needed it, but out of love for humankind. That is why the heavens declare not God's need but God's glory.

It is indeed said, "Our God is in heaven above," but this is said not as though God needed heaven, but as though he rests among the angels in heaven. Scripture often calls the angels in heaven "heaven," just as it calls the people of the earth "earth." So the historical narrative, hinting at the time of the midday meal, says, "And all the earth was eating its midday meal," meaning "It was the time for the midday meal." So it calls the people of the earth "earth" and the angels in heaven "heaven."

This is shown by the verse, "Let the heavens rejoice and let the earth be glad." Why should these beings in heaven, the angels, rejoice? Over the salvation of the world. And who vouches for this saying? The King of the angels himself, who says: "Truly, truly, I say to you, there is joy before all the angels in heaven over one sinner who repents."

Heaven came into being for God's glory but for our use, so that the sun might shine on us, and the moon and all the stars. God had no need of the sun. The Creator of light, who alone has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light, had no need of light perceived by the senses.

And it is no wonder that God has no need of sensible light, since not even the angels need earthly light, but only the heavenly; and the heavenly light is God himself. The book of Acts bears witness to this: "About midnight an angel appeared at the prison where Peter was." And what does the historian say, or rather the Holy Spirit who spoke through him? "And behold, an angel appeared in the night, and a light shone in the cell." If an angel, a created being, does not need light, does the Maker of the angels and of all creation need light? No, he does not need light; rather, through the light he gladdens us, gives us life, and warms us.

For all things came into being for his glory but for our use: the sun to shine on human beings, the clouds to serve by bringing rain, the earth to yield an abundance of fruits, and the sea to give merchants plenty. All things serve together on behalf of humankind, or rather on behalf of the image of God.

For when royal likenesses and portraits are brought into a city, and magistrates and people go out to meet them with acclamation and fear, they do this not to honor a wooden panel or a painting in wax, but the likeness of the emperor. In the same way creation does not honor the earthen vessel, but reveres the heavenly likeness.

So all things came into being not because God needed them, but for our use, and so that we might glorify God's love for humankind. That is why the Wisdom of God, bearing witness to God's mercy, said: "You have mercy on all, Lord, because you can do all things." From the beginning he made us out of love, and now he governs us with goodness. He would not have fashioned anything he hated: if he hated, he would not have formed us; if he hated, he would not have provided for us. That is why Scripture says: "You loathe nothing, Lord, of what you have made, for you would not have fashioned anything you hated."

So nothing in the visible world came into being because God needed it, but for God's glory, so that he might be glorified as the lover of humankind, who needs nothing and does all things. Even when we offer hymns to God or build houses for him, it is ourselves we honor and glorify; God receives only our gratitude. That is why David, who was grateful and loved God and valued gratitude above all, confessed that God lacks nothing, saying: "I said to the Lord, You are my Lord, for you have no need of my goods." For God needs nothing from us.

So the visible world proclaims God's goodness, but nothing proclaims it as much as his coming to dwell among human beings, so that he who was in the form of God came to be in the form of a servant, not changing his dignity but exalting his love for humankind. The awe-inspiring mystery that took place on this day leads our discourse to this subject. What happened on this day? The Savior washes the feet of his disciples.

In truth, it is awesome to speak of it and fearful to keep silent. We are afraid as we proclaim it, because we consider the greatness of his dignity; and we are afraid that by keeping silent we may fall into the danger of ingratitude. These things bring fear whether spoken or left unspoken: spoken, because of their greatness; left unspoken, because of the ingratitude. Let us then speak of these fearful things, since he himself did not decline to do these awesome things.

The Maker of human beings appeared on earth as a human being, the Master among servants, the Maker with the things he made, the form of God in the form of a servant. Of him Paul says: "Who, being in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant."

Throughout his whole human character, then, the Master of all put on the form of a servant. But he put on the form of a servant above all in this act of his saving plan, when he rose from supper: he who feeds all that is under heaven, when he reclined at table with the apostles, the Master with the servants, the fountain of wisdom with unlearned men, the Word with men who had not learned eloquence, the source of wisdom with men who did not know their letters; when he who feeds everyone reclined and dined with them, and he who feeds the whole world was fed together with his disciples.

And he was not content with this great gift of reclining at table with his own household servants. Peter, Matthew and Philip, men of the earth, reclined with him, while Michael and Gabriel and the whole army of angels stood by him. What a marvel! The one beside whom the angels stood in fear, the disciples reclined with in great freedom.

And he was not content with this marvel either. "Rising from supper," it says, he who covers himself with light as with a garment took off his outer robe; he who girds heaven with clouds girded himself with a towel; he who pours out the waters into lakes and rivers poured water into a basin. And kneeling down, he to whom every knee bends, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, washed the feet of his disciples.

The Lord of all washes the feet of the disciples, not insulting his own dignity but showing his boundless love for humankind. Yet great as this love was, Peter did not fail to recognize his Master's superiority. He who was always fervent in faith was found fervent also in his recognition of the truth. The others accepted his washing them, not indifferently but trembling, for it was not possible to contradict the Master. But Peter, out of reverence, does not let him, and says: "Lord, are you washing my feet? You shall never wash my feet."

Peter is rightly blunt: grateful, but not understanding the divine plan, he refuses out of faith and then obeys out of gratitude. The devout person ought to be like this: not unbending in his judgments, but yielding to the will of God. For though he spoke out as a man, he changed his mind as a lover of God. When the Savior saw his soul's resistance, unbending and harder than any anvil, he said to him: "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless I wash you, you have no share with me."

Notice how fearful the matter is, and how he broke down Peter's resistance with greater severity, pronouncing a severe sentence against him: he cuts him off from his own portion, so that human resistance may not prevail but God's will may prevail. Then the good and wonderful Peter, who had spoken out sharply, sharply changed his mind as well; and when he saw how severe the sentence was, he offered an equally decisive repentance, saying: "Not only my feet, but my hands and my head too! Wash all of me, cleanse all of me, so that I too may say with David, 'You will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.'" But the Savior said to him: "One who has bathed needs only to wash his feet."

And why does he wash only the feet? Because of the course the apostles were to run. He washes their feet not only to remove the dirt but also to put strength into the heels of the saints. Isaiah, seeing this beautiful foot-washing long ages before, and knowing that it was not a man who washed them but God who cleansed them, cried out: "How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news, of those who proclaim peace!" He touches their feet to strengthen earthly feet that were about to run through all that is under heaven.

And there is another mystery, brothers. In the beginning, when God pronounced sentence against Adam and Eve, he said to the serpent: "He will watch for your head, and you will watch for his heel." So he touches the place of the heel, against which the sentence was pronounced, so that once the Physician had laid his hand on it, the serpent's venom might no longer find a place there, and so that you may learn that the washing of the feet gave strength from then on against the demons. Before this the heel had been handed over to the serpent, but afterward, strengthened by the divine hand, it trampled on the deceiver. And as one who had made their feet strong, he says: "Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy."

Since, then, the cross of grace shines forth, and the Word of truth washes the minds of all of us, let us live in purity, sending up glory to him as our God who loves humankind, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
